title: Mapping and Monitoring Atmospheric Carbon Dioxide From NASA's OCO‐2 Satellite
content:
ABSTRACT

Carbon dioxide (CO2) is a leading greenhouse gas (GHG) and a principal driver of climate change. There is now an acceptance by almost all sectors of society that our planet's future climate is becoming hotter and more extreme, caused by GHGs in the atmosphere, particularly CO2. Since 2014, the NASA satellite Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 (OCO-2) has been continuously sensing CO2 concentrations over the globe. Mapping and monitoring CO2 at small-scale spatial and temporal resolutions allow carbon-cycle scientists to locate unusual behaviors, hypothesize causes, and revise climate projections. Aggregations of the satellite data to coarse yearly or large regional scales can limit answers to the “Where?” and “When?” questions needed for GHG mitigation. This article starts with OCO-2 retrievals on orbit tracks and demonstrates how to aggregate and filter them to display temporal and spatial signals, based on more than 7 years of OCO-2 data. One of the filters monitors the planet's progress toward “net zero by 2050.” Resampling-based inference highlights places in the space–time “cube” where the inter-annual and inter-regional variability of the carbon cycle is being disrupted, such as during El Niño/La Niña periods and the deceleration/acceleration of industrial activity as a result of the 2020–2021 COVID-19 pandemic.
